title: Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA walks through an agent-driven robotics workflow in which Hermes and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt on a local RTX Spark plan a Microduck obstacle course and the Astra agent builds 3D assets with FreeCAD and Blender. The course is assembled in Isaac Sim with Newton physics, a perception and locomotion policy is trained in Isaac Lab across 4,096 parallel environments on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, and validation runs back on RTX Spark. The post also covers sim-to-real preparation using Better Actuator Models and domain randomization.

insights.claim: In NVIDIA's Microduck workflow, the Hermes agent and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt running locally on RTX Spark turn a natural-language prompt into a step-by-step robotics project plan, review Microduck's documentation, generate a concept image of the course and inventory its reusable assets, then automatically hand the package off to the Astra agent.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is positioning its local hardware and Nemotron models as the orchestration layer for agentic robotics development.
insights.locator: 1. Create a plan of the obstacle course

insights.claim: NVIDIA's Astra agent creates 3D simulation assets by enhancing low-resolution reference crops with cloud image editing, checking them against the originals, building CAD geometry in FreeCAD and materials in Blender through programmatic execution, and exporting editable models and USD assets while logging unknown dimensions as modeling assumptions.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
insights.so_what: Agent-generated simulation assets could remove a major labor bottleneck in building robot training environments.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's SimReady Central Library offers more than 2,000 free, ungated simulation-ready OpenUSD assets that can be reused alongside newly generated objects in Isaac Sim.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
insights.so_what: Free content libraries deepen lock-in to NVIDIA's OpenUSD and Omniverse simulation ecosystem.

themes.theme: Simulation stack: Isaac Sim, Omniverse, Newton

insights.claim: In the Microduck workflow, Isaac Sim assembles the course and supplies Omniverse libraries for RTX rendering and sensor simulation, while Newton, an open-source GPU-accelerated physics engine, models the robot's movement, balance and ground contact.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
insights.so_what: Every layer of the physical-AI pipeline runs on NVIDIA GPU software, which expands GPU demand beyond LLMs into robotics simulation.

insights.claim: NVIDIA describes robot RL training as a loop where simulated observations drive policy actions, which produce simulated motion and updated observations, with rewards from unstable steps, collisions and falls guiding the policy toward success.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
insights.so_what: Simulation-heavy RL is compute-intensive, supporting demand for GPU workstations and cloud capacity among robotics developers.
insights.quote: Simulated observations → policy actions → simulated motion → updated observations
insights.locator: 4. Train the perception and locomotion policy

insights.claim: NVIDIA fine-tuned a pretrained Microduck locomotion policy to traverse ramps and obstacles in Isaac Lab using head-camera depth and robot-state observations, running 4,096 parallel environments on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition GPU.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
entities: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insights.so_what: Massively parallel RL on one workstation GPU lowers the barrier to robot training and creates a sales use case for RTX PRO Blackwell cards.
insights.quote: This adaptation run used 4,096 parallel environments on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition GPU.
insights.locator: The ramp and obstacle training experiment

insights.claim: NVIDIA's workflow combines local planning and asset generation, cloud-scale policy learning in Isaac Lab, and local policy validation in Isaac Sim on RTX Spark, where developers record course completion, falls, collisions and stall points from rollouts.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
insights.so_what: The hybrid local-plus-cloud pattern sells both NVIDIA edge and desktop devices and data-center GPU time.
insights.locator: 5. Validate the trained policy on RTX Spark

insights.claim: Isaac Lab supports Better Actuator Models (BAM) that simulate servo command delays, mechanical backlash and voltage drops from a shared battery, which can be matched to measurements from Microduck to narrow the sim-to-real gap.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
insights.so_what: Actuator fidelity is a key gating factor for low-cost robots trained in simulation and moving to real deployment.

insights.claim: Even with calibrated actuator models, sensors, ground contact and control timing differ on real robots, so Isaac Lab uses domain randomization of physical parameters and observation noise, and hardware tests still guide further rounds of training.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
insights.so_what: The sim-to-real gap is still unsolved, so physical-AI timelines depend on iterative real-world testing.
insights.locator: Even with a carefully calibrated model

insights.claim: Isaac Sim can run on NVIDIA RTX Spark using the Windows x86 binaries through Windows x86 emulation on Arm.
insights.speaker: Gabriele Leone
insights.so_what: Shows RTX Spark is an Arm-based Windows device relying on emulation for x86 software, a compatibility point to watch.
